specStatements.text: matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms and there are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atoms called elements
elements show periodic relationships in their chemical and physical properties
these periodic properties can be explained in terms of the atomic structure of the elements
atoms bond by either transferring electrons from one atom to another or by sharing electrons
the shapes of molecules (groups of atoms bonded together) and the way giant structures are arranged is of great importance in terms of the way they behave
there are barriers to reaction so reactions occur at different rates
chemical reactions take place in only three different ways:
energy is conserved in chemical reactions so can therefore be neither created or destroyed.

scopeNotes.statement: matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms and there are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atoms called elements
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification says 'about 100', so no item asks students to recall an exact count of naturally occurring elements, and no item requires the names, symbols or discovery of the synthetic elements. Items test the idea that a limited set of atom types builds all matter.

scopeNotes.statement: these periodic properties can be explained in terms of the atomic structure of the elements
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Explanations are kept to shells and outer-shell electrons, the level used elsewhere in 8462. No item requires sub-shells, orbitals, ionisation energy data or any quantum treatment of atomic structure.

scopeNotes.statement: the shapes of molecules (groups of atoms bonded together) and the way giant structures are arranged is of great importance in terms of the way they behave
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Items test that arrangement governs behaviour. No item asks students to name molecular shapes or state bond angles, and no item requires electron-pair repulsion theory, none of which appears in the 8462 specification.

scopeNotes.statement: there are barriers to reaction so reactions occur at different rates
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The barrier is treated qualitatively as a minimum energy needed for a collision to succeed. No item requires an activation energy to be calculated, and no item requires a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution to be drawn or interpreted.

scopeNotes.statement: energy is conserved in chemical reactions so can therefore be neither created or destroyed.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Conservation of energy is tested as a principle applied to reacting chemicals and their surroundings. No item requires enthalpy cycles, bond energy arithmetic or numerical energy change calculations, which belong to 4.5 rather than to this key idea.

concepts.definition: The tiny particle from which all matter is composed. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can still exist as that element.
A substance made of only one type of atom. There are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atom, so there are about 100 naturally occurring elements.
A pattern in which similar chemical and physical properties recur at regular intervals as the elements are listed in order of atomic number.
A vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons and so have similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row of the periodic table. Across a period the properties of the elements change, and that pattern of change repeats in the next period.
The electrons in the highest occupied energy level of an atom. They control how an atom bonds and reacts, so they are what the periodic patterns are explained by.
Bonding in which electrons are transferred from one atom to another, producing positive and negative ions that attract each other strongly.
Bonding in which two atoms share a pair of electrons, so that the shared pair is attracted to both nuclei at the same time.
A group of atoms bonded together. The shape of a molecule affects how it behaves, for example how closely molecules pack and how they fit other molecules.
A structure containing a very large number of atoms or ions joined by a repeating pattern of bonds, such as diamond, graphite or sodium chloride.
The minimum amount of energy that colliding particles must have in order to react. Collisions with less energy than this do not produce a reaction.
How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed. Under the same conditions, a reaction with a higher energy barrier is the slower one.
A reaction in which a hydrogen ion, H+, moves from one substance to another. Reactions of acids with alkalis are proton transfer reactions.
A reaction in which electrons move from one substance to another. The substance losing electrons is oxidised and the one gaining them is reduced.
A reaction in which atoms form covalent bonds by sharing pairs of electrons rather than by transferring them from one atom to another.
The principle that energy can be neither created nor destroyed. In a chemical reaction energy is only transferred, for example between the reacting chemicals and their surroundings.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the surroundings get hotter. No energy is created; it is transferred out of the chemical store.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the surroundings get colder. No energy is destroyed; it is transferred into the chemical store.

misconceptions.question: If there are only about 100 elements, how can there be millions of different substances?
misconceptions.correct: About 100 types of atom can be joined in a huge number of ratios and arrangements, and each different combination is a different substance.
misconceptions.misconception: There must only be about 100 different substances, because there are only about 100 different types of atom to make them from.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet 'about 100 elements' as a striking fact and read it as a limit on substances rather than a limit on ingredients. The combinatorial step, that a small set of building blocks gives an unlimited set of products, is rarely made explicit.
misconceptions.correction: Treat the elements as an alphabet. Twenty-six letters give an unlimited number of words; about 100 types of atom give millions of compounds, because atoms can join in different numbers, ratios and arrangements.

misconceptions.question: Does every element shown in the periodic table occur naturally?
misconceptions.correct: No. About 100 types of atom occur naturally; the remaining elements in the table have been made artificially in nuclear reactions.
misconceptions.misconception: Every element printed in the periodic table is one of the naturally occurring types of atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The periodic table is presented as one finished, authoritative object, so students assume nature supplies every box in it. The distinction between naturally occurring and synthetic elements is rarely drawn.
misconceptions.correction: Count the boxes in a full periodic table: there are more than 100. The specification says 'about 100 naturally occurring' precisely because the heaviest elements were made in laboratories, not found in rocks.

misconceptions.question: Does water contain a special 'water atom'?
misconceptions.correct: No. Water contains hydrogen atoms and oxygen atoms bonded together. There is no separate type of atom for each compound.
misconceptions.misconception: Each different compound must contain its own unique type of atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over the everyday idea that a new material needs a new ingredient. Particle diagrams that draw a compound as a single blob reinforce it.
misconceptions.correction: A compound is built from atoms of the elements it contains. Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. No new type of atom appears.

misconceptions.question: Do atoms turn into atoms of a different element during a chemical reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. Chemical reactions rearrange atoms and move electrons or protons; the atoms themselves are not changed into other elements.
misconceptions.misconception: New elements are made during chemical reactions, and that is where new substances come from.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Products often look nothing like the reactants, so students conclude the atoms themselves must have changed. Nuclear reactions met in physics lessons blur the boundary further.
misconceptions.correction: Check any balanced equation: the same atoms appear on both sides, only joined up differently. Changing one element into another needs a nuclear change, not a chemical one.

misconceptions.question: Does 'periodic' mean the properties change steadily from the first element to the last?
misconceptions.correct: No. Periodic means the pattern repeats: similar properties reappear at regular intervals as you move through the elements.
misconceptions.misconception: Periodic relationships form one smooth trend running all the way across the periodic table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught trends across a period and read them as a single global trend. The word 'periodic' is not connected to its everyday sense of happening again and again.
misconceptions.correction: Link 'periodic' to a repeating pattern, like the days of the week. Sodium behaves like lithium because the pattern has come round again, not because it is further along one line.

misconceptions.question: Which elements have similar chemical properties: those in the same period or the same group?
misconceptions.correct: Those in the same group, because their atoms have the same number of electrons in the outer shell.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements in the same period have similar properties, because the pattern is called 'periodic'.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'periodic' sounds as though it points to the periods. Rows and columns are also easily swapped when students read the table at speed.
misconceptions.correction: Periods are the rows; groups are the columns. Similar properties run down the columns. Sodium and potassium are both in Group 1 and both react vigorously with water.

misconceptions.question: Do periodic patterns apply to physical properties only?
misconceptions.correct: No. Chemical properties such as reactivity and physical properties such as melting point both show periodic relationships.
misconceptions.misconception: Only measurable physical properties such as melting point follow the periodic pattern.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Physical properties are the ones plotted on graphs, so they are the ones students see patterned. Chemical reactivity is taught separately as group chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: Group 1 reactivity increasing down the group and Group 7 reactivity decreasing down the group are chemical patterns. The specification names both chemical and physical properties.

misconceptions.question: Why do lithium, sodium and potassium react in similar ways?
misconceptions.correct: Because each of their atoms has one electron in its outer shell, so each reacts by losing that one electron.
misconceptions.misconception: They behave alike because their atoms contain the same number of electrons in total.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know electrons explain the similarity but reach for the total count, which is the number they have practised writing. That the totals differ here is not noticed.
misconceptions.correction: Write the electronic structures: Li 2,1; Na 2,8,1; K 2,8,8,1. The totals differ, but each ends in 1. It is the outer shell that governs chemical behaviour.

misconceptions.question: Do elements whose atoms have the same number of occupied shells behave alike?
misconceptions.correct: No. Atoms with the same number of occupied shells are in the same period, and their properties differ across that period.
misconceptions.misconception: Similar chemical behaviour comes from having the same number of electron shells.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Shells are the most visible feature of an atom diagram, so students use shell count as the point of comparison instead of outer-shell electron count.
misconceptions.correction: Sodium and chlorine both have three occupied shells, yet one is a reactive metal and the other a reactive non-metal. Compare the outer shells, not the number of shells.

misconceptions.question: Which particles are moved or shared when atoms bond?
misconceptions.correct: Electrons. Atoms bond by transferring electrons from one atom to another or by sharing electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Atoms bond by transferring or sharing protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Proton transfer is met as one of the three ways reactions happen, so students blur it with bonding. Protons and electrons are also easily confused as 'the charged bits'.
misconceptions.correction: Protons sit in the nucleus and stay there during bonding. Only outer electrons are transferred or shared when atoms bond to one another.

misconceptions.question: Do the nuclei of two bonded atoms join together?
misconceptions.correct: No. The nuclei stay separate and are held a fixed distance apart; the bond comes from the behaviour of the outer electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: A chemical bond is made by fusing or sticking the two nuclei together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday picture of things being glued together suggests the whole particles must join. Ball-and-stick models show two balls touching a rod, which looks like direct contact.
misconceptions.correction: In a covalent bond the shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei, holding the atoms a set distance apart. Joining nuclei would be a nuclear reaction, not a chemical one.

misconceptions.question: How do a metal and a non-metal bond together?
misconceptions.correct: By transferring electrons from the metal atom to the non-metal atom, producing oppositely charged ions.
misconceptions.misconception: All bonding involves sharing electrons, so a metal and a non-metal share electrons too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sharing is taught first and feels like the friendly, general case. Students then apply it everywhere instead of asking which types of element are involved.
misconceptions.correction: Metal with non-metal means transfer and ions; non-metal with non-metal means sharing and molecules. Magnesium oxide contains Mg2+ and O2-, not shared pairs.

misconceptions.question: In magnesium oxide, which atom loses the electrons?
misconceptions.correct: The magnesium atom loses two electrons to the oxygen atom, forming Mg2+ and O2-.
misconceptions.misconception: The oxygen atom gives its electrons to the magnesium atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxygen is described as the reactive, attacking element, so students assume it is the one doing the giving. The direction of transfer is often left unstated.
misconceptions.correction: Metals lose electrons; non-metals gain them. Magnesium has two outer electrons to lose, and oxygen needs two to fill its outer shell, giving MgO.

misconceptions.question: Does the behaviour of a substance depend only on which atoms it contains?
misconceptions.correct: No. How the atoms are bonded and arranged matters just as much as which atoms are present.
misconceptions.misconception: If two substances contain the same atoms then they must behave in the same way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Composition is the first thing students learn to read from a formula, so it becomes the whole explanation. Structure is treated as a picture rather than as a cause.
misconceptions.correction: Diamond and graphite both contain only carbon atoms, yet one is the hardest natural substance and the other is soft and conducts. The arrangement is the difference.

misconceptions.question: Is a giant structure just a very large molecule?
misconceptions.correct: No. A molecule is a fixed small group of bonded atoms; a giant structure is a continuous repeating lattice with no set number of atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Giant covalent substances such as diamond are simply enormous molecules with a formula like any other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are drawn as balls joined by sticks, and both involve covalent bonds, so the only apparent difference is size.
misconceptions.correction: Water is always H2O, three atoms. A diamond crystal has no set number of carbon atoms; the lattice just repeats, which is why melting it means breaking bonds throughout.

misconceptions.question: Does a substance need to contain a metal in order to conduct electricity?
misconceptions.correct: No. Graphite conducts because each carbon atom has a delocalised electron, even though no metal is present.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that conducts electricity must contain a metal somewhere in its structure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every conductor students handle, from wires to coins, is metallic, so conduction and metal become one idea.
misconceptions.correction: Conduction needs charged particles that are free to move. In graphite the delocalised electrons between the layers do that job, and graphite contains only carbon.

misconceptions.question: What is a 'barrier to reaction'?
misconceptions.correct: It is an energy requirement: colliding particles must have at least a minimum energy before they can react.
misconceptions.misconception: A barrier to reaction is a physical wall or layer keeping the reacting particles apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word barrier is concrete in everyday use. The oxide layer on magnesium ribbon is also called a barrier, which reinforces the physical reading.
misconceptions.correction: The barrier is a minimum energy, not an object. Even when particles are thoroughly mixed and colliding constantly, most collisions fail because they are not energetic enough.

misconceptions.question: Does every collision between reactant particles cause a reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only collisions with at least the minimum energy, and in a suitable direction, lead to a reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Particles react every time they collide, so the rate depends only on how often they collide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Collision theory is introduced through 'more collisions means faster', and the energy condition is dropped when students summarise it.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrogen and oxygen collide billions of times a second at room temperature yet barely react. A spark supplies the energy that gets collisions over the barrier.

misconceptions.question: Does a fast reaction always release more energy than a slow one?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rate and energy change are separate ideas. A slow reaction can release far more energy in total than a fast one.
misconceptions.misconception: The faster a reaction goes, the more energy it must give out overall.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Vigorous reactions look and sound energetic, so speed and energy are fused into a single idea of being powerful.
misconceptions.correction: Rusting is extremely slow but releases a large amount of energy overall. Rate depends on the size of the barrier; energy change depends on reactants and products.

misconceptions.question: Do neutrons take part in chemical reactions?
misconceptions.correct: No. Chemical reactions take place in only three ways: proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing.
misconceptions.misconception: Neutrons are transferred between particles as one of the ways reactions happen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Protons, neutrons and electrons are learnt as one list of three, so students assume all three are equally available to take part in reactions.
misconceptions.correction: Neutrons are locked in the nucleus and move only in nuclear changes. The specification names exactly three ways: proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing.

misconceptions.question: What is transferred when an acid is neutralised by an alkali?
misconceptions.correct: A proton, that is a hydrogen ion H+, is transferred from the acid to the alkali.
misconceptions.misconception: Neutralisation is an electron transfer reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electron transfer is the transfer students practise most, in redox and in ionic bonding, so it becomes the default answer whenever something is transferred.
misconceptions.correction: Acids supply H+ ions, and an H+ ion is simply a proton. Neutralisation is H+ + OH- giving H2O, which is proton transfer, not electron transfer.

misconceptions.question: In an acid and alkali reaction, which way does the proton move?
misconceptions.correct: From the acid to the alkali. The acid donates the hydrogen ion and the alkali accepts it.
misconceptions.misconception: The alkali donates a proton to the acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alkalis are described as the strong or aggressive partner in neutralisation, so students assume the alkali is the one giving something away.
misconceptions.correction: Acids are proton donors; bases and alkalis are proton acceptors. HCl gives its H+ to the OH- from sodium hydroxide, and water is formed.

misconceptions.question: Is neutralisation just the mixing and diluting of two solutions?
misconceptions.correct: No. A new substance, water, is formed and energy is released, so a chemical reaction has taken place.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding an alkali to an acid simply dilutes the acid until it is no longer acidic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both liquids look the same before and after, and adding water really does raise the pH of an acid, so dilution seems a sufficient explanation.
misconceptions.correction: The mixture warms up and a salt can be crystallised from it. Dilution on its own never produces heat or a new solid product.

misconceptions.question: Is energy used up and lost in a chemical reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. Energy is conserved. It is transferred between the chemicals and the surroundings, never destroyed.
misconceptions.misconception: Some energy is destroyed or used up during a reaction, which is why reactions eventually stop.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language talks of using up the energy in a battery or a fuel. Energy that has spread out into the surroundings is no longer useful, which students read as gone.
misconceptions.correction: Track where the energy went. When a fuel burns, energy stored in the chemicals has been transferred to the surroundings, which are now warmer. The total is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: Do exothermic reactions create energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. They transfer energy that was already stored in the chemicals out to the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: An exothermic reaction makes new energy, which is why the surroundings get hotter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy appears as warmth where there was none before, so making it seems the natural description, and 'gives out energy' sounds like production.
misconceptions.correction: Energy is neither created nor destroyed. The energy released was already in the chemical store of the reactants; the reaction only moves it to the surroundings.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about atoms and elements is correct?

options.text: Matter is made of atoms, and about 100 types of atom occur naturally.
options.rationale: Matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms, and there are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atom, which are the elements.

options.text: Matter is made of atoms, and about 100 substances exist in total.
options.rationale: Reads 'about 100' as a limit on substances rather than on types of atom, which would leave no room for the millions of known compounds.

options.text: Matter is made of atoms, and every element in the table is natural.
options.rationale: The periodic table holds more than 100 elements; the heaviest were made artificially, which is why the specification says 'about 100 naturally occurring'.

options.text: Matter is made of atoms, with one type of atom per compound.
options.rationale: Compounds contain atoms of the elements they are made from; no new type of atom is created when a compound forms.

mcqs.stem: There are only about 100 naturally occurring types of atom, yet chemists have identified millions of different substances. How is this possible?

options.text: Millions of other types of atom are still waiting to be discovered.
options.rationale: Assumes the number of substances must match the number of atom types, so extra atom types are invented to make the two numbers agree.

options.text: Those atoms can join in many different ratios and arrangements.
options.rationale: A limited set of atom types gives an unlimited set of compounds, because atoms can combine in different numbers, ratios and arrangements.

options.text: Atoms change into atoms of new elements when substances react.
options.rationale: Chemical reactions rearrange atoms; changing one element into another would require a nuclear change, not a chemical one.

options.text: Every new compound must contain its own new type of atom.
options.rationale: There is no 'water atom' or 'salt atom'; each compound is built from atoms of the elements it contains.

mcqs.stem: What does it mean to say that the elements show periodic relationships in their properties?

options.text: Properties change smoothly from the first element to the last one.
options.rationale: Treats the table as one continuous trend, which cannot explain why sodium behaves like lithium rather than like neon.

options.text: Only physical properties such as melting point follow a pattern.
options.rationale: The specification refers to chemical and physical properties; the reactivity trends down Groups 1 and 7 are chemical patterns.

options.text: Similar properties recur at regular intervals across the table.
options.rationale: Periodic means repeating: as the elements are listed in order, similar chemical and physical properties reappear at regular intervals.

options.text: Elements sharing a period have very similar properties.
options.rationale: Similar chemical properties run down the groups, which are the columns, not across the periods, which are the rows.

mcqs.stem: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react vigorously with water in a similar way. Which feature of their atomic structure explains this?

options.text: Their atoms all contain the same total number of electrons.
options.rationale: Lithium has 3 electrons, sodium 11 and potassium 19; the totals differ, so they cannot be the reason for the similarity.

options.text: Their atoms all have the same number of occupied shells.
options.rationale: Equal numbers of occupied shells would put the atoms in one period, where properties differ; these three lie in different periods.

options.text: Their atoms each have a different number of protons.
options.rationale: Different proton numbers are true of any three elements, so this cannot explain why these particular elements behave alike.

options.text: Each atom has just one electron in its outer shell.
options.rationale: Li is 2,1; Na is 2,8,1; K is 2,8,8,1. Each has a single outer electron to lose, so each reacts in the same way, which is why they share a group.

mcqs.stem: According to the key ideas, in what ways can atoms bond to one another?

options.text: By sharing electrons, or by fusing the two nuclei firmly together.
options.rationale: Nuclei stay separate in a chemical bond; joining them would be a nuclear change rather than a chemical one.

options.text: By transferring electrons from one atom to another, or by sharing them.
options.rationale: Atoms bond either by transferring electrons from one atom to another, which gives ions, or by sharing electrons, which gives covalent bonds.

options.text: By transferring protons between atoms, or by sharing protons.
options.rationale: Protons remain in the nucleus during bonding; only outer electrons are transferred or shared.

options.text: By sharing electrons only, since transfer is not bonding.
options.rationale: Sharing is generalised to every case, which cannot account for ionic compounds such as sodium chloride.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide, MgO. What happens to electrons as this compound forms?

options.text: Each magnesium atom shares its two electrons with an oxygen atom.
options.rationale: Sharing is applied to a metal and non-metal pair; magnesium oxide is ionic and contains Mg2+ and O2- ions.

options.text: Each oxygen atom transfers two electrons to a magnesium atom.
options.rationale: The direction of transfer is reversed. Metals lose electrons and non-metals gain them, so oxygen is the receiver here.

options.text: Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to an oxygen atom.
options.rationale: Magnesium has two outer electrons to lose and oxygen needs two to fill its outer shell, giving Mg2+ and O2- ions in MgO.

options.text: Each magnesium atom gives two protons to an oxygen atom.
options.rationale: Protons cannot leave the nucleus in a chemical reaction; transferring them would turn magnesium into a different element.

mcqs.stem: Why do the key ideas say that the shapes of molecules and the arrangement of giant structures are of great importance?

options.text: Because the shape of a substance decides only how it looks to us.
options.rationale: Reduces structure to how a substance looks, whereas the specification says arrangement governs the way substances behave.

options.text: Because two substances made of the same atoms always behave alike.
options.rationale: Composition is treated as the whole explanation, which cannot account for diamond and graphite being so different.

options.text: Because a giant structure is really just a very big molecule.
options.rationale: A molecule has a fixed small number of atoms; a giant structure is a continuous repeating lattice, and the two behave very differently.

options.text: Because how the particles are arranged decides how they behave.
options.rationale: Structure is a cause, not a picture: how atoms are bonded and arranged controls properties such as hardness, melting point and conductivity.

mcqs.stem: Diamond and graphite are both giant structures containing only carbon atoms, yet graphite is soft and conducts electricity while diamond is hard and does not. Why?

options.text: The carbon atoms are bonded in different arrangements.
options.rationale: Same atoms, different structure: graphite forms layers with delocalised electrons, while diamond is a rigid three-dimensional network.

options.text: Graphite holds a small amount of metal that carries the current.
options.rationale: Conduction is assumed to need a metal; graphite is pure carbon and conducts through its own delocalised electrons.

options.text: Graphite contains a softer type of carbon atom than diamond does.
options.rationale: There is no soft variety of carbon atom. The atoms are identical; only the way they are joined together differs.

options.text: Graphite is a molecule, so it is not a giant structure.
options.rationale: Graphite is a giant covalent structure with no fixed number of atoms, not a molecule with a set formula.

mcqs.stem: The key ideas state that there are barriers to reaction. What does this mean?

options.text: Reacting particles are kept apart by a physical layer between them.
options.rationale: Takes 'barrier' literally as an object; the barrier is still there in a thoroughly mixed solution where particles collide constantly.

options.text: Substances have to be melted before their particles can react.
options.rationale: Many reactions happen between solids or gases well below their melting points, so melting is not the barrier.

options.text: Colliding particles need a minimum amount of energy before they react.
options.rationale: The barrier is an energy requirement. Collisions below that energy do not lead to reaction, so different barriers give different rates.

options.text: Every collision between particles will produce a reaction.
options.rationale: If every collision worked there would be no barrier at all, and every reaction would be instant.

mcqs.stem: Two different reactions are carried out at the same temperature and concentration, but one goes much more slowly than the other. What best explains the difference?

options.text: A physical barrier keeps its particles apart in the flask.
options.rationale: Reads the barrier as a solid obstacle rather than as the energy needed for a collision to succeed.

options.text: The slower reaction releases less energy overall than the faster.
options.rationale: Confuses rate with energy change. Rusting is very slow yet releases a large amount of energy in total.

options.text: Its particles are colliding much less often than the other.
options.rationale: At the same temperature and concentration the collision frequency is similar; what differs is the fraction of collisions that succeed.

options.text: The slower reaction has the higher energy barrier to overcome.
options.rationale: A higher barrier means a smaller fraction of collisions carry enough energy to react, so fewer collisions succeed and the rate is lower.

mcqs.stem: The key ideas state that chemical reactions take place in only three different ways. What are those three ways?

options.text: Proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing.
options.rationale: These are exactly the three ways given in the specification, covering acid reactions, redox reactions and the formation of covalent bonds.

options.text: Proton transfer, neutron transfer and electron transfer only.
options.rationale: Adds neutrons to the list because the three sub-atomic particles are learnt together; neutrons move only in nuclear changes.

options.text: Proton sharing, neutron sharing and electron transfer only.
options.rationale: Mixes the particles with the processes; protons are transferred rather than shared, and neutrons take no part at all.

options.text: Electron transfer, energy transfer and proton sharing.
options.rationale: Energy transfer accompanies every reaction rather than being one of the three ways, and protons are transferred, not shared.

mcqs.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide solution. In terms of the three ways reactions take place, what happens here?

options.text: An electron is transferred from the acid to the hydroxide ions.
options.rationale: Electron transfer is the default answer for many students, but in neutralisation it is H+ that moves, not electrons.

options.text: A proton is transferred from the acid to the alkali.
options.rationale: The acid donates H+, which is simply a proton, to the OH- ions from the alkali, forming water. This is proton transfer.

options.text: A proton is transferred from the alkali across to the acid.
options.rationale: The direction of transfer is reversed. Acids are proton donors and alkalis are proton acceptors.

options.text: The two solutions only mix and dilute one another here.
options.rationale: The mixture warms up and a salt can be crystallised from it, so a new substance has certainly been formed.

mcqs.stem: A strip of zinc is placed in copper sulfate solution. The blue colour fades and copper is deposited on the zinc. Which of the three ways of reacting is this?

options.text: Electron sharing, because zinc and copper share electrons here.
options.rationale: Sharing is generalised to two metals in solution, but ions are formed and discharged, which requires transfer.

options.text: Proton transfer, because zinc gives protons to copper ions.
options.rationale: Protons stay in the nucleus; transferring them would turn zinc into another element altogether.

options.text: No transfer at all; the copper simply drops out of solution.
options.rationale: The fading colour shows Cu2+ ions are being removed from the solution, which is a chemical change, not settling.

options.text: Electron transfer, because zinc atoms lose electrons to copper ions.
options.rationale: Zn loses two electrons to become Zn2+, and Cu2+ gains them to become copper metal, so this is electron transfer.

mcqs.stem: Which of these changes is an example of electron sharing?

options.text: Two hydrogen atoms bond together to form a hydrogen molecule.
options.rationale: Two non-metal atoms bond by sharing a pair of electrons, which forms the covalent bond in H2.

options.text: Sodium and chlorine atoms react to form solid sodium chloride.
options.rationale: A metal reacting with a non-metal transfers electrons and forms ions; it does not share them.

options.text: A magnesium atom loses two electrons and becomes an ion.
options.rationale: Losing electrons is transfer, the other way in which atoms bond, rather than sharing.

options.text: An acid reacts with an alkali to give a salt and water.
options.rationale: Neutralisation is proton transfer, which is one of the other two ways reactions take place.

mcqs.stem: What does it mean to say that energy is conserved in chemical reactions?

options.text: Reactions that give out heat create the energy that they release.
options.rationale: Energy appears as warmth where there was none, so students describe it as made; in fact it was already in the chemical store.

options.text: Energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred.
options.rationale: This is the principle stated in the specification: energy is conserved, so a reaction can only move energy between stores.

options.text: Energy is gradually used up, which is why reactions stop.
options.rationale: Everyday talk of using up energy is taken literally; reactions stop when a reactant runs out, not when energy is destroyed.

options.text: Reactions that take energy in destroy some of what they absorb.
options.rationale: Energy taken in from the surroundings is stored in the products, not destroyed.

mcqs.stem: During a reaction in an open beaker, the mixture and the beaker both become noticeably hotter. What has happened to the energy?

options.text: The reaction has created new energy as the products formed.
options.rationale: Energy cannot be created; the warmth comes from energy already stored in the reactants.

options.text: Some of the energy was destroyed as the new bonds formed.
options.rationale: Making bonds releases energy to the surroundings; no energy is destroyed in the process.

options.text: It has all been transferred out to the surroundings.
options.rationale: The reaction is exothermic: energy stored in the chemicals has been transferred out to the mixture, the beaker and the air, which is conservation, not creation.

options.text: It was stored in the beaker before and has now escaped.
options.rationale: The beaker is not an energy source; it warms up because energy is transferred into it from the reacting chemicals.
